title: “TWO FALSE PROPHETS WERE ACCUSED OF COMMITTING ADULTERY WITH THEIR NEIGHBORS’ WIVES”
paragraphs: “TWO FALSE PROPHETS WERE ACCUSED OF COMMITTING ADULTERY WITH THEIR NEIGHBORS’ WIVES”
They spoke in God’s name. People listened to them. But behind the prophetic voices was a secret God had already seen. — Jeremiah 29:21–23
There are sins people hide from other people.
And then there are sins people try to hide behind God.
That second kind should terrify us.
Because Jeremiah 29 contains a story many Christians have probably passed over without realizing how disturbing it actually is.
Two men were speaking as prophets.
They used the name of God.
People were listening.
Their names were Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah.
And according to the Lord’s accusation through Jeremiah, while these men were supposedly speaking for God, they were committing adultery with the wives of their neighbors.
Read that again slowly.
Men who claimed to carry words from heaven were living secret lives that contradicted the holiness of the God whose name they invoked.
And God knew.
The Hebrew text of Jeremiah 29:21 describes them:
הַנִּבְּאִים לָכֶם בִּשְׁמִי שָׁקֶר
Hannibbe’im lakhem bishmi shaqer.
In context: they were prophesying falsely to the people in God’s name.
That last part matters.
They were not merely lying.
They attached God’s name to the lie.
Then Jeremiah 29:23 pulls back the curtain:
יַעַן אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ נְבָלָה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל וַיְנַאֲפוּ אֶת־נְשֵׁי רֵעֵיהֶם
Ya‘an asher ‘asu nevalah beYisra’el, vayena’afu et-neshei re‘eihem.
Because they had committed נְבָלָה — nevalah in Israel.
A disgraceful, outrageous, morally shameful thing.
And Scripture becomes painfully specific:
וַיְנַאֲפוּ — vayena’afu.
They committed adultery.
With whom?
נְשֵׁי רֵעֵיהֶם — neshei re‘eihem.
The wives of their companions or neighbors.
These were not allegations invented centuries later to destroy somebody’s reputation. This is the accusation recorded in the biblical text itself.
But the most frightening sentence may still be coming.
God says:
וְאָנֹכִי הַיּוֹדֵעַ וָעֵד
Ve’anokhi hayyodea va‘ed.
In essence:
“I am the One who knows, and I am witness.”
That sentence changes everything.
Because somebody reading this right now knows what it is like to maintain two versions of yourself.
There is the version everybody sees.
And there is the version that appears when nobody is watching.
There is the worship version.
And the browser-history version.
The Sunday version.
And the midnight version.
The person who raises hands in worship...
and the person who cannot stop returning to pornography.
The person posting Bible verses...
and secretly messaging somebody else’s husband or wife.
The person telling everybody, “God told me”...
while ignoring what God has already plainly said.
The person serving at church...
while jealousy, lust, bitterness, dishonesty, pride, greed, or unforgiveness quietly eats through the soul.
Maybe your hidden thing is nothing like the sin of Ahab and Zedekiah.
But you still know what hiding feels like.
You know what it feels like to delete something.
Close something.
Rename something.
Minimize something.
Explain something away.
Promise God you will never do it again...
then find yourself standing in the same darkness three weeks later.
And perhaps nobody knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your church does not know.
Your followers certainly do not know.
But Jeremiah gives us four words we desperately need to recover:
God knows. God is witness.
That sounds terrifying.
And if we stop with Jeremiah 29, terror may be all we feel.

Ahab and Zedekiah were not presented as repentant men desperately fighting sin. They were false prophets whose deception and sexual immorality stood under divine judgment. Jeremiah says God would hand them over to Nebuchadnezzar, and their end would become proverbial among the Jewish exiles.
This passage therefore gives us no permission to turn grace into an excuse.
Grace does not mean sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely how seriously sin matters.
Something has happened in modern Christianity when people can become more afraid of being exposed than of becoming corrupted.
We fear screenshots more than sin.
We fear losing followers more than losing integrity.
We fear somebody discovering what we did more than grieving the God before whom we did it.
And sometimes we become experts at Christian vocabulary while our private lives slowly collapse.
That is one of the warnings buried inside Jeremiah 29.
Spiritual language cannot sanctify rebellion.
Saying “God told me” does not make something God’s will.
Having a platform does not make somebody a prophet.
Charisma is not character.
Influence is not holiness.
An audience is not divine approval.
And perhaps most importantly...
being able to hide something from people does not mean it is hidden from God.
“I am the One who knows, and I am witness.”
Those words should follow us into every locked room.
Every private conversation.
Every hotel room.
Every secret account.
Every financial decision.
Every ministry meeting.
Every flirtation we tell ourselves is harmless.
Every thought we keep feeding while pretending we want it to die.
Every time we use spiritual language to justify something Scripture has already condemned.
God knows.
But here is where the Gospel takes us somewhere extraordinary.
The same God from whom sin cannot hide is the God before whom sinners do not have to keep hiding.
That difference is everything.
Ahab and Zedekiah warn us about hypocrisy and unrepentant rebellion.
But Jesus Christ shows us what God does with sinners who come into the light.
Think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Her scandal was no longer private.
There was no reputation left to protect.
No carefully constructed public image.
She stood exposed.
Religious accusers surrounded her.
Her sin was real.
Her shame was real.
And Jesus did something astonishing.
He did not call evil good.
He did not redefine adultery.
He did not pretend holiness no longer mattered.
He extended mercy and called her away from sin.
That is grace.
Not:
“Your sin does not matter.”
But:
“Your sin does not have to be your master anymore.”
Jesus does not rescue us so we can become comfortable inside the prison.
He opens the prison.
He calls us out.
This is why repentance is beautiful.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the moment you finally stop defending what is destroying you.
It is dropping the mask.
Opening the locked door.
Bringing the secret into the light.
Calling sin what God calls it.
Turning around.
Coming home.
And discovering that Jesus already knew the worst chapter before you finally admitted it existed.
Maybe that is what somebody needs to hear tonight.
Jesus already knows.
The affair.
The addiction.
The lies.
The messages.
The secret resentment.
The compromise.
The relapse.
The pride.
The double life.
The thing you hope nobody ever discovers.
He knows.
And yet the Gospel invitation still stands.
Not an invitation to remain unchanged.
An invitation to repent, believe, receive mercy, and begin walking in a new direction.
The apostle John writes that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us (1 John 1:9).
Paul writes that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1).
And Scripture says that anyone in Christ is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).
Notice the movement.
Confession.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
New creation.
That is Christianity.
Not learning how to hide more successfully.
Becoming new.
Maybe you have spent years believing Christianity means convincing everybody you have your life together.
It does not.
Christianity begins with admitting that you don't.
We needed a Savior because we could not save ourselves.
And His name is Jesus.
At Calvary, Christ did not die for an imaginary, cleaned-up version of you.
He died for sinners.
He carried sin.
He bore judgment.
He shed His blood.
He rose from the grave.
And now forgiveness is offered to those who turn to Him in faith.
So there is something more frightening than having your scandal exposed.
It is protecting your scandal until it destroys you.
And there is something more beautiful than successfully protecting your reputation.
It is finally becoming free.
Perhaps Jeremiah 29:23 found you because there is something you need to stop hiding.
Not necessarily publicly.
Wisdom matters. Privacy matters. Other people's dignity matters. Confession does not mean broadcasting intimate details to the internet.
But you can stop hiding from God.
You can seek trustworthy pastoral accountability.

If another person has been harmed, genuine repentance may require truth, responsibility, boundaries, restitution where appropriate, and accepting consequences rather than using “grace” to escape them.

And if sexual abuse, coercion, exploitation, or criminal conduct is involved, protecting victims and involving appropriate authorities must never be replaced by merely keeping the matter “inside the church.”
Real repentance does not manipulate forgiveness.
Real repentance tells the truth.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs to become painfully simple:
“Jesus, no more hiding.”
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It doesn't.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that you need Christ becomes the first small crack in a wall you have spent years building.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed person finally believes restoration is possible.
Not because Gospel Warrior needs another meaningless statistic on a screen.
Someone needs to remember:
God sees the secret...
but Jesus still calls sinners into the light.
There is also another way to help this ministry continue.
Scripture teaches willing generosity, not manipulated giving.
But voluntary financial support can help Gospel ministry continue.
That costs nothing.
One share can travel somewhere we cannot.

One share can enter a hospital room, a broken marriage, a lonely bedroom, a struggling believer's midnight, or the phone of somebody quietly wondering whether Jesus could possibly forgive what they have done.
And if God has enabled you to support financially, consider doing so freely and prayerfully.
Not from guilt.
Not because somebody promised prosperity.
But because you genuinely want to help the Gospel travel farther.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the person who has wandered.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
Let them encounter Scripture.
Let them wrestle with Jesus.
Let the Word do what only the Word can do.
Because Jeremiah's warning still speaks.
You can fool an audience.
You can fool friends.
You can fool family.
You can build an entire reputation around a person you are not.
But eventually every mask meets the eyes of the God who says:
“I know. I am witness.”
And yet for the repentant sinner, those words do not have to be the end of the story.
Because the God who sees you completely is the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
So come into the light.
Not when you become worthy.
Now.
Bring Christ the chapter you wanted erased.
Bring Him the failure you cannot rewrite.
Bring Him the chains you cannot break alone.
Bring Him the truth.
Because maybe the greatest miracle is not that Jesus prevents every scandal.
Maybe sometimes the miracle is that after sin has wrecked everything we thought we were...
Jesus begins writing something grace alone could produce.
The secret God already knows may become the very place where grace finally teaches you to stop running.
